title: The Hidden Coin Toss in Every Pea: How Mendel Found the Rules of Inheritance
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

intro.summary: Mendel asked whether the offspring of hybrid plants follow a regular, countable law. Over eight years he crossed garden pea varieties that differed in sharp either-or characters, such as round versus wrinkled seeds, and counted many thousands of offspring over several generations. He found that one character hides in the hybrid but returns unchanged in about one in four of its offspring. That 3:1 split is really 1:2:1, and separate characters combine independently. He explained all of this by proposing that a hybrid makes two kinds of egg and pollen cells in equal numbers, which pair up by chance. His main limits: the work covered peas and a few bean crosses, used only sharply defined characters, and relied on averages that fluctuate in small samples. His flower-colour results in beans did not fit simply, and he himself asked for the key experiments to be repeated.
background: A hybrid is the offspring of two plants that differ in some visible character, for example a cross between a tall pea and a short pea.
Pea flowers normally fertilise themselves, so a breeder can control exactly which pollen reaches which flower.
Every seed starts when one pollen cell joins one egg cell, so each parent passes something to the offspring through these cells.
In Mendel's day many breeders expected hybrids to be blends of their parents, and expected the offspring of hybrids to vary without any clear rule.
intro.aha: A character that vanishes in a hybrid returns unchanged in one in four of its offspring because the hybrid makes two kinds of egg and pollen cells in equal numbers that pair by chance, and crossing hybrids back to a parent gave the near-equal groups this predicts.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Breeders had long noticed that crossing the same two plants gives the same hybrid every time. Nobody had found a law for what happens in the generations after that. Mendel argued that earlier experiments were too small or too loosely organised to count the different offspring forms and track them generation by generation.
primer.quote: not one has been carried out to such an extent and in such a way as to make it possible to determine the number of different forms under which the offspring of hybrids appear, or to arrange these forms with certainty according to their separate generations, or to definitely ascertain their statistical relations

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: He tested 34 pea varieties for two years to make sure each one bred true, then kept 22. He picked seven characters that come in two clearly different forms, such as round or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green seed interiors, and tall or short stems. He crossed varieties in both directions and let the hybrids fertilise themselves. Then he counted every offspring, often thousands per character, and followed some lines for up to six generations.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: The hybrid always looked like one parent: that character he called dominant, and the hidden one recessive. In the next generation the hidden character came back unchanged in about a quarter of the plants. Over all seven characters the average ratio was 2.98 to 1. By growing on the dominant-looking plants he found that two thirds of them were secretly hybrids, so the 3:1 was really 1 constant dominant : 2 hybrids : 1 constant recessive. With two or three characters at once, the forms combined as if each character followed its own separate rule.
primer.quote: this occurs in the definitely expressed average proportion of three to one, so that among each four plants of this generation three display the dominant character and one the recessive.
primer.quote_where: The First Generation [Bred] from the Hybrids

primer.heading: His explanation
primer.body: Mendel proposed that a hybrid makes two kinds of egg cells and two kinds of pollen cells, one for each parental character, in equal numbers. Which pollen meets which egg is left to chance. On average this gives one quarter pure dominant, one half hybrid and one quarter pure recessive. He tested the idea by crossing hybrids back to a parent, and the predicted forms appeared in nearly equal numbers.
primer.quote: It remains, therefore, purely a matter of chance which of the two sorts of pollen will become united with each separate egg cell.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: A messy question about resemblance became a counting problem with exact predictions. The idea of discrete units that are passed on unchanged later became the foundation of genetics. Mendel was careful about the limits. His ratios hold only on average and can swing widely in a single plant. He used only sharp either-or characters. A bean cross with flower colour did not fit simply, and he explained it only by a hypothesis. He asked others to repeat his key experiments.
primer.quote: Even the validity of the law formulated for Pisum requires still to be confirmed, and a repetition of the more important experiments is consequently much to be desired

concepts.title: The hybrid looks like only one parent
concepts.idea: When two true-breeding peas that differ in one character are crossed, the hybrid shows one parent's form (dominant) and hides the other (recessive), whichever parent supplied the pollen.

terms.means: A variety whose offspring always look like it in a given character, generation after generation
The parental form that shows in the hybrid, entire or almost unchanged
The parental form that disappears from view in the hybrid
Making the same cross both ways, so each variety serves once as the seed parent and once as the pollen parent

concepts.recap: In a cross between two true-breeding pea forms, the hybrid wears only the dominant form, and it makes no difference which parent gave the pollen.

understand.explanation: Mendel started with pea varieties that were true-breeding: he grew them for two trial years and each kept giving offspring like itself. Each pair he crossed differed clearly in one character, such as round versus angular seeds. The hybrid did not look halfway between its parents: in all seven characters it resembled one parent so closely that the other parent's form could not be seen. He called the form that shows in the hybrid dominant and the form that vanishes recessive. For every pair he also made a reciprocal cross, swapping which variety gave the pollen, and the hybrid looked the same either way. Caveats: this held for seven sharply defined pea characters; he notes that ornamental-plant hybrids were often intermediate for traits like leaf shape, and that long-by-short pea hybrids often grew even taller than the long parent.
understand.quote: Henceforth in this paper those characters which are transmitted entire, or almost unchanged in the hybridisation, and therefore in themselves constitute the characters of the hybrid, are termed the dominant, and those which become latent in the process recessive.

activities.prompt: Mendel made every cross in both directions. Compare a cross between round-seeded and angular-seeded peas with its reciprocal cross. Does it matter which plant gives the pollen?

cases.label: Round plant gives the egg cells
cases.text: Flowers of a true-breeding round-seeded pea are opened, their stamens are removed, and they are dusted with pollen from an angular-seeded pea. The hybrid seeds are round.

cases.label: Angular plant gives the egg cells
cases.text: Now the roles are swapped: the angular-seeded pea is the seed bearer and the round-seeded pea supplies the pollen. The hybrid seeds are again round, with no visible trace of the angular form.

cases.label: What an expert can tell
cases.text: Mendel cites Gärtner's remark that even the most practised expert cannot tell from a hybrid which of the two parents was the seed plant and which was the pollen plant.

activities.takeaway: The paper states that 'it is perfectly immaterial whether the dominant character belong to the seed-bearer or to the pollen parent; the form of the hybrid remains identical in both cases.' Dominance belongs to the form itself, not to the mother or the father.

activities.title: Dominant or recessive?
activities.prompt: Each card names one form of a pea character and says what Mendel's hybrids looked like. Use the definition: the form the hybrid shows is dominant, and the form that vanishes is recessive.

cards.text: Round seeds. Crossing round-seeded with angular-seeded peas gave hybrids with round seeds.
cards.feedback: Dominant. The hybrid shows the round form, so round is the dominant form of seed shape.

cards.text: Green seed interior. Crossing yellow-interior with green-interior peas gave hybrids with yellow interiors.
cards.feedback: Recessive. The green interior disappears in the hybrid, which shows yellow.

cards.text: Green unripe pods. Crossing green-podded with yellow-podded peas gave hybrids with green pods.
cards.feedback: Dominant. Here green is the form that shows. Green is dominant for the pod but recessive for the seed interior, so a colour is not dominant in itself. Each character has to be tested.

cards.text: White seed-coat with white flowers. Crossing these with grey-brown-coated, violet-flowered peas gave grey-brown coats and violet flowers.
cards.feedback: Recessive. The white coat and white flowers vanish in the hybrid.

cards.text: Pods pinched in between the seeds. Crossing these with simply inflated pods gave hybrids with inflated pods.
cards.feedback: Recessive. The hybrid shows the inflated pod, so the pinched (constricted) pod is hidden.

cards.text: Flowers spread along the stem. Crossing these with flowers bunched at the top gave hybrids with flowers along the stem.
cards.feedback: Dominant. The hybrid shows flowers along the stem, and the bunched-at-the-top form is hidden.

cards.text: Long stem. Crossing 1 ft and 6 ft plants gave hybrids between 6 ft and 7½ ft tall.
cards.feedback: Dominant. The hybrid is long-stemmed, often even longer than the long parent. Mendel suggests this extra growth may come from the vigour seen when very different stems are crossed. It is not a blend of the two heights.

activities.takeaway: In all seven pea characters the hybrid showed one parental form and hid the other. Which form wins depends on the character, not on a rule such as 'green always wins'.
hints: Ask of each card: which form does the hybrid actually display?
If the card's form is the one the hybrid shows, it is dominant. If the hybrid shows the other form, it is recessive.
Watch the two green cards: they belong to different characters and land in different groups.

activities.question: A gardener uses a true-breeding short-stemmed pea as the seed plant and dusts it with pollen from a true-breeding long-stemmed pea. Going by Mendel's results, what will the hybrid look like?

options.text: Short, like the seed plant, because the plant that bears the seed passes on its form
options.feedback: Mendel made every cross both ways and found that it makes no difference which parent bears the seed. The long stem is dominant from either side.

options.text: Long-stemmed, like the pollen parent
options.feedback: Right. The long stem is dominant, and the hybrid looks the same whichever parent gave the pollen. Mendel even found that such hybrids often outgrew the long parent.

options.text: About halfway between the two heights
options.feedback: For these sharply defined pea characters Mendel saw no blending. A 1 ft by 6 ft cross gave hybrids of 6 to 7½ ft, not about 3½ ft.

options.text: Some hybrids short and some long, half and half
options.feedback: The hybrids from such a cross all looked alike. Mixed forms appear only among the hybrids' own offspring, which is the next part of the story.

hints: Which stem length is dominant?
Does it matter which parent supplied the pollen?

activities.question: Mendel describes a cross where the seed plant had a short stem, white flowers bunched at the top, and inflated pods. The pollen plant had a long stem, violet-red flowers along the stem, and pinched pods. In which character did the hybrid resemble the seed plant?

options.text: Only in pod form
options.feedback: Right. Of the seed plant's forms, only the inflated pod is dominant. In stem length and in flower colour and position, the hybrid took the pollen plant's dominant forms. Mendel reports exactly this.

options.text: In all three characters, because it grew on the seed plant
options.feedback: Growing on the seed plant gives it no advantage. The hybrid shows whichever form is dominant, and the long stem and violet flowers along the stem came from the pollen plant.

options.text: Only in stem length
options.feedback: The seed plant's short stem is recessive, so it is hidden. The hybrid had a long stem like the pollen plant.

options.text: In none of them; it looked entirely like the pollen plant
options.feedback: Not quite. The pollen plant's pinched pod is recessive, so in pod form the hybrid showed the seed plant's inflated pod.

hints: Go through each character and ask which of the two forms is dominant.
Only one of the seed plant's three forms appeared in your 'dominant' group in the sort.

concepts.title: The hidden character returns: 3 to 1, on average
concepts.idea: When hybrids self-fertilise, the recessive form reappears in about one in four offspring. That 1-in-4 share settles down only over large counts; small batches swing widely.

predict.question: Two gardeners repeat Mendel's round × wrinkled cross and let the hybrids pollinate themselves. Gardener A counts one plant's 40 seeds and finds one third wrinkled. Gardener B pools 4,000 seeds and also finds one third wrinkled. Which result is a real problem for the one-in-four rule?
options: Neither: one third is close enough to one quarter
why: A small count can look like the odd one out, but with 40 seeds the hump is wide. One third sits well inside the usual scatter, as Mendel's 14-and-15 plant showed for a far bigger miss.
Right: with 4,000 seeds the hump is a narrow spike around one quarter. A share of one third lies far outside it, so luck can't explain it. Something other than chance is going on.
The two shares are the same, but batch size changes how far chance can push them. The same miss is ordinary for 40 seeds and nearly impossible for 4,000.
For 40 seeds, yes. For 4,000 seeds, no: big counts pin the share within about a percentage point of one quarter, so an eight-point miss is not 'close enough'.

terms.means: A flower's own pollen fertilises its own egg cells, as peas normally do inside the closed keel
How far a single count wanders from the true share just by the luck of which seeds formed
Three dominant-looking offspring for every one recessive, so the recessive share is one quarter

model.title: How the wrinkled share of a batch scatters around one in four
model.note: Teaching model: each seed is treated as an independent chance event with a one-in-four chance of being wrinkled. The scatter of batch shares is drawn with a smooth bell-shaped approximation, which is rough for very small batches. The batch-size slider moves in steps of 5 seeds, so some of Mendel's counts are rounded by a seed. The seed totals 7,324 and 8,023 and the single-plant counts (14 round with 15 wrinkled; 43 round with 2 wrinkled) are Mendel's. The curve and the percentages are illustrative, not his data.

controls.label: Share wrinkled in a marked batch

outputs.label: Chance a batch lands at least this far from ¼

x.label: Share of the batch's seeds that are wrinkled (the hidden form)

series.label: Where batches of this size land

steps.say: Take a hybrid pea that looks round but hides the wrinkled form. Along the bottom: what share of a batch of its seeds comes out wrinkled, from none to all.
The hump shows where batches of this size usually land. Taller means more common. The shaded part holds 95 of every 100 batches.
This line marks one seed in four.
This slider sets how many seeds are in the batch. Watch the hump change.
This slider places one real batch on the picture. The box below says how often chance alone lands a batch that far from one in four.

explore.prompt: You've seen single plants scatter and big totals settle. Now find the batch sizes yourself.

goals.text: Make the batch big enough that 95 of every 100 batches land within 2 percentage points of one quarter.
hints: Which slider makes the hump narrower?
Watch the 'Middle 95% spans ±' box as you add seeds. Doubling the seeds does not halve the spread, so you need more than you might think.
The answer lies between one and three thousand seeds, well below Mendel's own totals.

goals.text: Mark a batch that is just over half wrinkled, like the plant with 14 round and 15 wrinkled seeds. Then find a batch size where a share that extreme counts as ordinary: inside the middle 95%.
hints: Big batches pin the share near one quarter. Which way should the seed count go?
Put the marker near one half first. Then change the batch size and watch the 'chance' box climb past 5%.
Think of a single pod rather than a whole plant.

feedback.correct: Yes. The same share means different things at different batch sizes. Forty seeds scatter widely, so one third is unremarkable. Four thousand seeds hug one quarter so tightly that one third can't be luck.
feedback.incorrect: You may have judged each share on its own, without its batch size. The model says chance scatter shrinks as counts grow. A miss that is routine for one plant becomes impossible for thousands of seeds, and only then does it challenge the rule.

steps.say: Start with the hybrid letting its own pollen fertilise its flowers. This is self-fertilisation, which peas do naturally. Count just 4 seeds: the hump is so wide that almost any share of wrinkled seeds is possible.
A single pod holds about six to nine seeds. Mendel often found pods where every seed was round. Mark zero wrinkled in 9 seeds: chance does this in roughly one pod in ten.
Now a whole plant of 29 seeds. Mendel reports one with 14 round and 15 wrinkled, over half wrinkled. That sits far out in the tail: roughly a one-in-a-thousand plant.

And the opposite tail: another plant, with about 45 seeds, gave 43 round and only 2 wrinkled. Both plants are rare, but Mendel grew hundreds of plants, so a few odd ones are expected. This luck-driven wobble is called fluctuation.
Now pool everything. In his first experiment Mendel counted 7,324 seeds from 253 hybrids. The hump collapses to a spike: the fluctuations of single plants cancel out.
He found 1,850 wrinkled, 25.3%, or 2.96 round for every wrinkled seed. Across all seven characters the average was 2.98 to 1: the 3 : 1 ratio.

Last, mark the 14-and-15 plant's share against a batch the size of his second experiment (8,023 seeds). The chance falls to zero: odd for one plant, impossible in a big count. That is why the totals reveal the rule.

understand.explanation: When Mendel let his hybrids self-fertilise, the hidden recessive form came back unchanged in the next generation, in about one offspring in four: three dominant to one recessive. Across his seven characters the pooled ratios ran from 2.82 to 3.15 to 1, with an overall average of 2.98 to 1. Single plants were far less tidy: one gave 43 round and 2 wrinkled seeds, another 14 round and 15 wrinkled. The model shows how both can be true at once. If each seed is a separate chance event, small batches scatter widely while large totals settle close to one quarter. Mendel himself pointed to his big seed experiments as the ones that fix the average, and the model treats his extreme plants as rare tail cases of chance, not as breaks in the rule.
understand.quote: These two experiments are important for the determination of the average ratios, because with a smaller number of experimental plants they show that very considerable fluctuations may occur.
understand.quote_where: The First Generation [Bred] from the Hybrids

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not an equation from the paper. Mendel gives the centre, an average of 3 : 1, so one quarter is recessive, and observes that fewer plants fluctuate more. The ¼ is the one-in-four line. The green part is the 'Middle 95% spans ±' box. The blue n is the seeds-counted slider: because n sits under a square root, you need four times the seeds to halve the scatter.

concepts.recap: The recessive form returns in about one offspring in four, but only large counts show that cleanly; single pods and plants swing widely by chance.

concepts.title: Two thirds of the 'dominant' plants are secret hybrids
concepts.idea: Growing on the dominant-looking offspring shows that one third breed true and two thirds split 3:1 again, so the 3:1 is really 1 pure dominant : 2 hybrids : 1 pure recessive.

terms.means: A plant whose offspring all show its own form, generation after generation. Mendel calls such forms 'constant'.
Telling identical-looking plants apart by growing their offspring and seeing what appears.
Mendel's shorthand: A is a pure dominant form, a is a pure recessive form, and Aa is a hybrid carrying both.

concepts.recap: Looks can hide what a plant carries. Testing the offspring splits the 3 dominant-looking plants into 1 pure plant and 2 hidden hybrids, giving 1 : 2 : 1, or A + 2Aa + a.

understand.explanation: When hybrids self-fertilise, about three in four offspring show the dominant form, but they do not all carry the same thing inside. Mendel ran a progeny test: he grew each dominant-looking plant on to see whether it breeds true, giving only offspring like itself, or splits. About one third bred true, while about two thirds split into dominant and recessive at 3 to 1, just like the original hybrids; recessive-looking plants always bred true. So the 3 : 1 is really 1 pure dominant : 2 hybrids : 1 pure recessive, which in Mendel's shorthand A, Aa, a (pure dominant, hybrid, pure recessive) reads A + 2Aa + a. These are averages: his largest trial gave 193 true-breeding plants to 372 splitting ones (1.93 to 1), and his smaller trials of 100 plants wandered further from 2 to 1.
understand.quote: It is therefore demonstrated that, of those forms which possess the dominant character in the first generation, in two-thirds the hybrid character is embodied, while one-third remains constant with the dominant character.
understand.quote_where: The Second Generation [Bred] from the Hybrids

activities.question: Self-fertilised hybrids give about 3 plants with the dominant form for every 1 with the recessive form. All the dominant-looking plants look the same. What share of them do you think are secretly still hybrids?

options.text: None: they look pure, so they are pure
options.feedback: A natural first guess, since nothing on the outside hints at a hidden character. Hold on to it and see whether the offspring agree.

options.text: About one third
options.feedback: A possible guess. Keep it in mind while you watch what Mendel's plants did when he grew them on.

options.text: About half
options.feedback: A tempting middle answer. You will be able to check it against Mendel's counts shortly.

options.text: About two thirds
options.feedback: A possible guess. Keep it in mind and compare it with the counts that follow.

options.text: All of them
options.feedback: A possible guess if you think the hybrid nature never goes away. Watch what their offspring reveal.

activities.prompt: Follow Mendel's progeny test one step at a time.

stages.label: 1. The puzzle
stages.text: Among the offspring of the hybrids, three in four show the dominant form. Mendel saw that this form could mean two things: a parental character, which should pass unchanged to all offspring, or a hybrid character, which should split again. Only the next generation could tell which.

stages.label: 2. The recessives
stages.text: First, the easy group. Plants showing the recessive form were grown on, and their offspring kept the recessive form. They bred true without exception.

stages.label: 3. The big trial (seed shape)
stages.text: Mendel grew 565 plants from round seeds. 193 gave only round seeds, so they bred true. 372 gave both round and angular seeds, in about 3 to 1, just like the original hybrids.

stages.label: 4. Checking the other characters
stages.text: Seed colour gave 166 true-breeding plants to 353 splitting ones. For the other five characters he took 100 dominant-looking plants and grew ten seeds of each. The splits were 36/64, 29/71, 40/60, 33/67 and 28/72 (true/splitting). The 40/60 trial was repeated and gave 35/65.

stages.label: 5. Reading the result
stages.text: Every trial lands near 1 true-breeding plant for every 2 hidden hybrids. The small trials of 100 plants scatter more, as small counts do. So the 3 dominant-looking plants are really 1 pure dominant + 2 hybrids, and with the 1 pure recessive the series is A + 2Aa + a.

activities.takeaway: Identical-looking dominant plants come in two hidden kinds, and their own offspring are what tell them apart.

activities.question: In the seed-shape trial, 372 plants split and 193 bred true. How many splitting plants is that for each true-breeding plant? (Give the ratio as one number.)
hints: Divide the number of splitting plants by the number of true-breeding plants.
372 is a little under twice 193.
activities.explanation: 372 ÷ 193 ≈ 1.93, the figure Mendel reports. The seed-colour trial gave 353 ÷ 166 ≈ 2.13. He noted that the two together come almost exactly to 2 to 1, and that the smaller trials varied more, as expected with only 100 plants.

activities.title: What do the offspring reveal?
activities.prompt: These are illustrative plants, not records from the paper. Sort each one by what its offspring show about it.

cards.text: A round-seeded plant whose seeds are all round
cards.feedback: No angular seeds appear, so this plant breeds true for the dominant form: one of the one-third group.

cards.text: A round-seeded plant whose seeds are round and angular, about 3 to 1
cards.feedback: It looks dominant, but it splits just like the original hybrids. That makes it one of the hidden two thirds.

cards.text: An angular-seeded plant whose seeds are all angular
cards.feedback: Recessive-looking plants always bred true in Mendel's trials, so this is a pure recessive.

cards.text: A plant with green unripe pods whose offspring include some with yellow pods
cards.feedback: Green pods are dominant. Yellow-podded offspring show the plant was carrying the hidden recessive form, so it is a hybrid.

cards.text: A tall plant whose ten offspring all grew tall
cards.feedback: Mendel counted plants like this as constant. One caveat: with only ten offspring, a hybrid could by chance give ten tall ones (about a 6% chance, since 0.75 multiplied by itself ten times ≈ 0.056). Small tests can occasionally misclassify a plant.

cards.text: A plant with flowers along the stem whose offspring include some with flowers bunched at the top
cards.feedback: Flowers along the stem are dominant. Offspring with top-bunched flowers reveal a hidden recessive, so this plant is a hybrid.

cards.text: A white-flowered plant whose offspring are all white-flowered
cards.feedback: White flowers are the recessive form. A plant that shows it has nothing hidden and breeds true.

activities.takeaway: A plant that looks recessive is always pure. A plant that looks dominant can only be classified by its offspring.

activities.question: Back to your first guess. Among the dominant-looking offspring of self-fertilised hybrids, about what share are hidden hybrids?

options.text: None: they look pure, so they are pure
options.feedback: Looks mislead here. In every character tested, most dominant-looking plants split again when grown on, so many were hybrids.

options.text: About one third
options.feedback: This swaps the two groups. About one third bred true; the other two thirds were the hybrids (193 true vs 372 splitting in the largest trial).

options.text: About half
options.feedback: Half of all offspring are hybrids, which is the 2 in 1 : 2 : 1. Among the dominant-looking plants alone, though, it is 2 out of 3.

options.text: About two thirds
options.feedback: Right. Of the 3 dominant-looking plants in every 4 offspring, 1 is pure and 2 are hybrids, so the full series is A + 2Aa + a. Real counts scatter around this (1.93 to 1 and 2.13 to 1 in the largest trials).

options.text: All of them
options.feedback: If all were hybrids, none would breed true. Yet about one third gave only dominant offspring, 193 of 565 in the seed-shape trial.

concepts.title: Characters combine like separate dice
concepts.idea: When hybrids differ in several characters, each character follows its own 1:2:1 rule independently, so the forms multiply: 3^n kinds, 2^n true-breeding kinds, out of 4^n equally weighted offspring.

predict.question: A gardener crosses two pea varieties that differ in five clear characters, then keeps growing the hybrids' offspring. How many different kinds that breed true in every character could she eventually find?
why: 10 comes from adding two pure forms per character (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2). The characters multiply, they don't add.
25 is 5 × 5, as if the number of characters were being squared. The rule is 2 choices per character, raised to the number of characters.
Right: each character has 2 pure forms (A or a), and the choices combine freely, so 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^5 = 32.
243 is 3^5, the number of all kinds of offspring, including those that are still hybrid in some character. Only 32 of them breed true in all five.

terms.means: One character's outcome tells you nothing about another's. Seed shape and seed colour are sorted separately, like two dice rolled together.
Mendel's name for the full list of offspring forms you get by multiplying each character's A + 2Aa + a series together

model.title: How many forms the offspring of a hybrid can take
model.note: Teaching model: it counts the averages Mendel's rule predicts. It assumes each character follows A + 2Aa + a on its own and that every offspring in one full set is equally likely. Real counts swing by chance, as Mendel's did. The formulas are Mendel's. The plant numbers you choose are illustrative, though the walkthrough quotes counts he reported.

controls.label: Number of characters the parents differ in
Plants raised from the hybrids' seed

outputs.label: Share of offspring that breed true in every character
Share exactly like the seed parent
Plants expected exactly like the seed parent

steps.say: These bars count the offspring of a hybrid pea that fertilises itself: how many different kinds appear, how many of those breed true, and how big one full set is.
The last bar is the one offspring in each full set that is exactly like the seed parent.
This slider sets how many characters the two parents differ in. Watch the bars jump.
This slider sets how many plants you grow from the hybrids' seed.
This box tells you how many of those plants you should expect to match the seed parent exactly.

explore.prompt: Now use the multiplication rule yourself. Predict where each threshold falls before you move the sliders.

goals.text: Find the fewest differing characters for which fewer than 1 in 10 offspring breed true in every character.
hints: With one character, half the offspring (A and a) breed true. What happens to that share each time you add a character?
Each extra character halves the share. Watch the 'breed true in every character' box as you step the first slider.
Start from 50% and count how many halvings it takes to get under 10%.

goals.text: Raise as many plants as the model allows, then find the fewest differing characters for which you would expect less than one plant exactly like the seed parent.
hints: Two things set the expected count: how many plants you grow and how rare an exact copy is.
Expected copies = plants ÷ size of one full set. Push the plants slider to its top first.
Then step the characters up one at a time. Stop at the first setting where the expected count drops below one.

feedback.correct: Yes. Each character contributes 2 pure forms, and the choices combine freely. Five characters give 2^5 = 32 true-breeding kinds out of 3^5 = 243 kinds in all.
feedback.incorrect: The counts don't add up character by character, and they don't count only the kinds that look different. Each character offers 2 pure forms, and independent characters multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

steps.say: Start with one character, as before. The hybrid's offspring come as A + 2Aa + a: 3 kinds, 2 of which breed true, in a full set of 4 (1 + 2 + 1).
Now let the parents differ in seed shape and seed colour. Any of the 3 shape kinds can go with any of the 3 colour kinds, so there are 3 × 3 = 9 kinds in a full set of 4 × 4 = 16.
Mendel found exactly these nine forms among 529 plants. The groups averaged 33, 65 and 138 plants, close to the 1 : 2 : 4 the rule predicts.
Multiplying only works if the characters are independent: a seed's shape tells you nothing about its colour. Mendel's counts showed exactly that.
Three characters: 27 kinds, 8 that breed true, a full set of 64. Mendel grew 639 plants and found all 27. The groups averaged 10, 19, 43 and 78, close to 1 : 2 : 4 : 8.
This full list, built by multiplying each character's series, is what Mendel called the combination series. Notice that the share breeding true in every character halves with each step.
Now seven characters, with 200 plants. There are 2187 kinds in a full set of 16,384. An exact copy of a parent is 1 in 16,384, so you would expect almost none among 200 plants.

understand.explanation: Each character sorts itself into A + 2Aa + a on its own, whatever the other characters do. So the possibilities multiply. Each extra character triples the kinds of offspring, doubles the kinds that breed true and quadruples the size of one full, equally weighted set. Mendel showed this with two-character and three-character crosses: all 9 and all 27 predicted forms appeared, in counts close to the predicted 1 : 2 : 4 and 1 : 2 : 4 : 8. By repeated crossing he also obtained all 128 (2^7) true-breeding combinations of his seven characters. The counts are averages that fluctuate by chance in small samples. Mendel showed the rule for the pea characters he tested and asked for the experiments to be repeated. 'Exactly like a parent' means alike in every character and breeding true. Because of dominance, many more plants can merely look like a parent.
understand.quote: the offspring of the hybrids in which several essentially different characters are combined represent the terms of a series of combinations, in which the developmental series for each pair of differentiating characters are associated. It is demonstrated at the same time that the relation of each pair of different characters in hybrid union is independent of the other differences in the two original parental stocks.
understand.quote_where: The Offspring of Hybrids in which Several Differentiating Characters are Associated

check.task: Recreate Mendel's three-character experiment. Get the model to show 27 kinds of offspring, and raise enough plants that each true-breeding kind (such as an exact copy of the seed parent) is expected about 10 times, which is the average Mendel observed.
check.hint: Kinds triple with each character, so find the setting that gives 27. Each true-breeding kind turns up once per full set, so you need about ten full sets of plants.
check.misconception: Treating characters as if their forms add up (3 + 3 + 3 = 9 kinds) instead of multiplying, or forgetting that the full set grows fourfold per character, so the plants needed grow fast too.

connect.caption: Mendel's own counting rule. n (the first slider) is the number of differentiating characters. The coloured results match the bars: 3^n terms of the combination series, 2^n unions that remain constant, and 4^n individuals in one full, equally weighted set. They come from multiplying A + 2Aa + a once per character: 3 terms, 2 constant terms and 4 individuals each time.

concepts.recap: Independent characters multiply: n differences give 3^n kinds, 2^n true-breeding kinds and 4^n offspring per full set, so an exact parent copy quickly becomes rare.

concepts.title: Two kinds of cells, equal numbers, paired by chance
concepts.idea: If a hybrid makes egg cells and pollen cells of two kinds in equal numbers and they pair at random, the offspring are one quarter pure dominant, one half hybrid and one quarter pure recessive: exactly the 1:2:1 that looks like 3:1.

predict.question: Imagine a hybrid pea (Aa for seed shape) whose pollen cells are half A and half a, but whose egg cells carry A three times as often as a. Pairing is still by chance. About what share of its seeds would be angular (pure a)?
why: Tempting because 1 in 4 is the familiar result. But 1 in 4 needs both egg and pollen cells split evenly. Here only a quarter of the eggs carry a, so fewer a-eggs are available to meet a-pollen.
Right. A pure a seed needs an a-egg (1 in 4 of eggs) to meet an a-pollen cell (1 in 2 of pollen). Chance pairing multiplies the shares: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.
This would need both kinds of cell to be lopsided: 1/4 × 1/4. The pollen is still half a, so only the egg side shrinks the angular share.
Fewer a-eggs is not the same as no a-eggs. As long as some eggs and some pollen carry a, chance will sometimes bring them together.

terms.means: A grid of every egg type against every pollen type, with one box for each possible meeting. The name is later; Mendel wrote the pairings as fractions.
Any egg is as likely to meet one pollen cell as another, so the share of a pairing is the egg share times the pollen share.

model.title: How a hybrid's egg and pollen cells meet: seeds per 100 from each meeting
model.note: Teaching model: one character (seed shape, round A over angular a) and one self-fertilising hybrid. The grid gives exact average shares, with none of the chance swings that real counts show. Letting egg and pollen shares differ is a what-if: Mendel assumed both are half and half. Unequal settings are illustrative, not the paper's data. The equal-share result is the paper's A + 2Aa + a.

controls.label: Share of egg cells carrying A
Share of pollen cells carrying A

steps.say: This grid is a hybrid pea making seeds. Each row is a kind of egg cell, and each column is a kind of pollen cell.
This slider sets what share of the egg cells carry round (A). The rest carry angular (a).
This one does the same for the pollen cells. Watch the boxes recolour.
Each box shows how many of every 100 seeds come from that egg meeting that pollen cell.
These totals add up the boxes into pure round, hybrid and pure angular seeds, and count how many look round.

explore.prompt: Play with how the hybrid shares out its cells. Watch which kinds of seeds the grid produces.

goals.text: Make the hybrid's seeds split exactly into Mendel's A + 2Aa + a: one quarter pure round, one half hybrid, one quarter pure angular.
hints: Mendel's assumption was about how many of each kind of cell the hybrid makes. Neither kind should win.
Both sliders matter: the pure angular box is the egg-a share times the pollen-a share.
For pure angular to be one quarter with both sides alike, each a-share must be the number that, multiplied by itself, gives one quarter.

goals.text: Keep hybrids at exactly half of the seeds, but make pure round and pure angular come out unequal.
hints: Hybrids come from two routes: an A egg with a pollen, and an a egg with A pollen.
Try keeping one kind of cell evenly split and moving only the other slider.
With the eggs half and half, every pollen share gives hybrids exactly one half. So where does the tilt show up?

feedback.correct: Yes. Chance pairing multiplies shares: an a-egg (1/4) meets a-pollen (1/2) 1/8 of the time. Only equal numbers on both sides give the 1 in 4 that Mendel saw.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed the 1 in 4 is fixed. In this model it comes from multiplying two halves. Change either side's share and the angular share changes with it: here 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.

steps.say: Start with Mendel's assumption: the hybrid makes egg cells half A and half a, and pollen cells half A and half a.
This grid has a later name: a Punnett square. Each box is one possible meeting of an egg and a pollen cell.
Pairing is by chance, which we call random union. So a box's share is the egg share times the pollen share: half of a half, or 25 seeds in 100.
An A egg with A pollen gives pure round, 25 in 100. An a egg with a pollen gives pure angular, also 25.
The other two boxes both make a hybrid, Aa. Two routes lead there, so hybrids get 50 in 100: one, two, one.
Hybrids look round, because A is dominant. So 75 in 100 look round and 25 look angular. The hidden 1:2:1 shows up as 3:1.
Now tilt the hybrid to make more A cells. Pure angular drops to 9, and about 91 look round. That is roughly 10 to 1, nothing like Mendel's 2.98 to 1.
Back to equal numbers. Only here does the grid give exactly A + 2Aa + a, the series Mendel had counted.

understand.explanation: Mendel asked what a hybrid's reproductive cells must be like to produce the pattern of 1 pure : 2 hybrid : 1 pure. His answer had two parts. First, the hybrid makes egg and pollen cells carrying A or a in equal numbers. Second, which pollen meets which egg is pure chance. Then each of the four meetings is equally likely. A with A and a with a give pure plants, and the two mixed meetings both give hybrids. That is A + 2Aa + a, which dominance makes look like 3:1. If the numbers were unequal, the 3:1 would break, as the grid shows. Mendel stressed that this holds only on average. Single plants and pods fluctuate, so the true ratio appears only in large counts. He treated the idea as a hypothesis to be tested by experiment.
understand.quote: It remains, therefore, purely a matter of chance which of the two sorts of pollen will become united with each separate egg cell. According, however, to the law of probability, it will always happen, on the average of many cases, that each pollen form A and a will unite equally often with each egg cell form A and a

check.task: Put the model in a state where pure round and pure angular seeds come out in equal numbers, yet hybrids are not half of the seeds.
check.hint: Pure round grows with the A shares, and pure angular grows with the a shares. Try making the egg cells lean one way and the pollen cells lean the other way by the same amount.
check.misconception: That if the two pure forms come out equal, the hybrid must have made its cells in equal numbers. Balanced pure forms alone do not prove the full 1:2:1: the hybrid share must also be one half.

connect.caption: This is Mendel's own bookkeeping. Each fraction is one meeting, with the pollen cell above the line and the egg cell below. A/A (pure round) and a/a (pure angular) are the two pure boxes in the grid. A/a and a/A are the two hybrid boxes, which together make 2Aa. With equal numbers of each kind of cell, each fraction is one quarter.

concepts.recap: Equal numbers of A and a cells, paired by chance, give A + 2Aa + a. Dominance makes that look like 3:1, and unequal numbers would break it.

concepts.title: The test: cross the hybrid back to a parent
concepts.idea: Crossing a hybrid with the pure recessive parent supplies only one kind of pollen, so the offspring directly show the hybrid's egg types. Mendel found near-equal groups (31, 26, 27, 26), confirming equal numbers of each kind.

predict.question: A breeder has a round-seeded pea. She can't tell whether it is pure round or a hidden hybrid. She fertilises it with pollen from a pure angular plant and grows 40 seeds. If it is a hybrid, what should she see?
why: All round is what a pure round plant would give, because every egg carries A. A hybrid also makes eggs carrying a, and these show up as angular seeds.

Right. The angular pollen adds only a, so each seed's look copies its egg: A eggs give round hybrids and a eggs give angular seeds. Equal egg types give roughly 20 and 20, with some chance wobble in a batch of 40.
3 to 1 is what you get when a hybrid fertilises itself, because both sides then carry A half the time. Here the pollen side never carries A.
1 in 4 angular needs a from both egg and pollen by chance. Here the pollen always supplies a, so only the egg decides, and half the eggs carry a.

terms.means: Crossing a hybrid with one of its pure parents, here the pure recessive one
Two kinds of offspring in equal numbers

model.title: How a hybrid's egg and pollen cells meet: seeds per 100 from each meeting
model.note: Teaching model: one character (seed shape, round A over angular a). The grid gives exact average shares, with none of the chance swings that real counts show. The switch replaces the hybrid's own pollen with pollen from the pure angular parent, which all carries a. Mendel's own test followed two characters at once (shape and colour), giving four groups; here one character gives two. Unequal egg or pollen shares are what-ifs, illustrative and not the paper's data. The counts quoted in the lesson (31, 26, 27, 26 and others) are the paper's.

controls.label: Share of egg cells carrying A
Share of pollen cells carrying A
Pollen all from the pure angular parent

outputs.label: Hybrid (Aa)
outputs.expr: pe * (1 - (1 - back) * pp) + (1 - pe) * (1 - back) * pp

steps.say: Same grid as before. Egg cells run down the side and pollen cells across the top. Each box shows the seeds per 100 that come from that meeting.
One thing is new: this switch. Turn it on, and the hybrid no longer fertilises itself. All its pollen now comes from the pure angular parent.
That pollen only ever carries a, so the left column empties and the pollen slider stops mattering. Keep an eye on the round and angular boxes.

explore.prompt: Use the switch and the egg slider to read a hybrid's egg cells straight off its seeds.

goals.text: With the pollen coming from the pure angular parent, make round-looking and angular seeds come out in equal numbers
hints: In this cross, what decides whether a seed looks round or angular?
All the pollen carries a, so a seed looks round only when its egg carried A. The round share simply copies one slider.
Turn the switch on, then move only the egg slider until the round and angular boxes match.

goals.text: With the pollen still from the pure angular parent, find the egg mix that would make round seeds outnumber angular ones 3 to 1
hints: In this cross, the round share is a direct readout of something inside the hybrid.
To get 3 round for every angular seed, which kind of egg must the hybrid make three times as often as the other?
Keep the switch on and move only the egg slider. The pollen slider does nothing here, so watch the round box.

feedback.correct: Yes. Pure angular pollen adds only a, so each seed's look copies its egg. A hybrid's eggs are half A and half a, which gives about half round and half angular seeds.
feedback.incorrect: You may be picturing the hybrid fertilising itself, which gives 3 to 1. In this cross the pollen side always carries a. Only the egg decides each seed's look, and a hybrid's eggs are half and half.

steps.say: Start where the last idea left off. A hybrid fertilises itself, and half its eggs and half its pollen carry A. One seed in four is pure angular, and three in four look round.
But the round-looking seeds are a mix of pure round and hybrid. Counting them can't show the egg cells directly. The 3 to 1 blends egg and pollen meeting by chance.
Mendel's fix was to fertilise the hybrid's flowers with pollen from the pure angular parent. Every pollen grain now carries a. This is a back-cross: crossing a hybrid with one of its pure parents.
Now no seed can be pure round. An egg carrying A makes a round-looking hybrid, and an egg carrying a makes an angular seed. The seeds read out the eggs one for one: 50 round, 50 angular.
Check that it really is a readout. If a hybrid made 70% A eggs, 70% of the seeds would look round. The pollen slider no longer matters at all.
Equal eggs predict equal groups: a 1:1 ratio. Mendel tracked shape and colour. Hybrid eggs crossed with angular green pollen gave 31, 26, 27 and 26 seeds. For shape alone: 57 round, 53 angular.
He also reversed the cross, putting hybrid pollen on angular green flowers. That gave 24, 25, 22 and 27. The hybrid's pollen came half and half too.

Now switch back to self-fertilising. A vanished character returns in one seed in four because the hybrid makes two kinds of egg and pollen in equal numbers, paired by chance. The back-cross showed those equal numbers.

understand.explanation: A self-fertilised hybrid gives 3 to 1, but that count blends egg and pollen meeting by chance, so it can't show the egg cells directly. Crossing the hybrid with the pure recessive parent fixes the pollen side: every grain carries a. Each seed's look then copies its egg, so the offspring are a direct count of the hybrid's egg types. If the two kinds are made in equal numbers, the groups should be about equal. Mendel ran this test in both directions, on hybrid eggs and on hybrid pollen. He got near-equal groups such as 31, 26, 27, 26 and 24, 25, 22, 27. They were not exactly equal: with about a hundred seeds per experiment, chance swings are expected, and some seeds failed to grow.
understand.quote: In all the experiments, therefore, there appeared all the forms which the proposed theory demands, and also in nearly equal numbers.

connect.caption: This is the model's one-character rule. When all pollen carries a, the round share equals the share of eggs carrying A (the egg slider), and the angular share equals the rest. Mendel wrote the two-character version: egg cells AB, Ab, aB, ab meeting pollen ab give AaBb, Aab, aBb, ab in equal numbers if the egg types are equal.

concepts.recap: Crossing a hybrid with the pure recessive parent turns its offspring into a direct count of its egg types. Mendel's near-equal groups showed that the two kinds come in equal numbers.

activities.question: In another test, Mendel crossed a plant hybrid for flower colour with one hybrid for stem length. For each character, that is a hybrid meeting a pure recessive. The theory predicted four equal classes. He counted 47, 40, 38 and 41 plants (166 in all), with violet flowers in 85 and white in 81. What should we conclude?

options.text: The counts support the theory: they are close to equal, and differences this size are expected by chance with 166 plants.
options.feedback: Supported. The theory predicts equal shares on average, not exact equality. Mendel himself stressed that small samples swing, and he judged the theory 'satisfactorily confirmed' here.

options.text: The counts refute the theory, because 47 and 38 are not equal.
options.feedback: This expects chance to deliver perfect averages. Which pollen meets which egg is a matter of chance, so a batch of 166 will wobble around 41 or 42 per class.

options.text: The counts prove the eggs and pollen are exactly half and half in every single plant.
options.feedback: Too strong. Mendel notes the assumption 'does not require that this should apply to each separate hybrid with mathematical exactness'. The counts fit equal numbers on average.

options.text: Nothing can be said, because the classes should have been 3 to 1.
options.feedback: 3 to 1 is the pattern when a hybrid fertilises itself. Here each character is a hybrid crossed with a pure recessive, so equal classes are the prediction.

hints: What did the theory predict for each class, and how many plants were counted?

activities.question: Which passage states the principle that the cross-back experiments confirmed?

options.quote: The law of combination of different characters which governs the development of the hybrids finds therefore its foundation and explanation in the principle enunciated, that the hybrids produce egg cells and pollen cells which in equal numbers represent all constant forms which result from the combinations of the characters brought together in fertilisation.
options.feedback: Yes. This is the principle the cross-back tests checked: hybrids make each kind of egg and pollen cell in equal numbers.

options.quote: Those forms which in the first generation maintain the recessive character do not further vary in the second generation as regards this character; they remain constant in their offspring.
options.feedback: True and important, but it describes recessive-looking plants breeding true. It says nothing about the hybrid's cells coming in equal numbers.

options.quote: It was furthermore shown by the whole of the experiments that it is perfectly immaterial whether the dominant character belong to the seed-bearer or to the pollen parent; the form of the hybrid remains identical in both cases.
options.feedback: This is about how the hybrid looks, whichever parent gave the pollen. It is not the principle about equal numbers of egg and pollen cells.
